 ```yaml
 ---
 
 # Markdown Instructions
 
 These instructions define the Markdown style guide...
 ```
 <!-- </example-frontmatter-instructions> -->
 
 ## Lists
 
 * Use unordered list markers consistently across a file; for the same level, do not mix `*`, `+`, `-`.
   * Try to always use `*` for unordered lists.
   * Avoid using `-` and `+` for unordered lists unless the file already uses these.
 * Indent unordered sublist content by 2 spaces per level.
 * Keep indentation consistent for items at the same nesting level.
 * Use one space between any list marker and the list text for both ordered and unordered lists.
 * Surround lists with a blank line before and after (unless at file start/end).
 * For ordered lists, either use `1.` for all items or increment numerically; do not mix styles within a list. Leading zeros are allowed only when used consistently.
 
 <!-- <example-lists> -->
 ```markdown
 * Item 1
 * Item 2
   * Nested item
 
 1. Step
 2. Step
 3. Step
 ```
 <!-- </example-lists> -->
 
 ### Bullet point punctuation
 
 Follow professional editorial standards for bullet point punctuation consistency:
 
 * **Fragment bullet points** (short phrases, technical terms, simple commands): Do NOT end with periods.
 * **Complete sentence bullet points** (subject + verb constructions): End with periods.
 * Based on Google, Microsoft, and GitLab style guidelines
 
 <!-- <example-bullet-punctuation> -->
 ```markdown
 * Configuration file
 * API endpoint
 * User authentication
 * Enable debugging mode
 
 * This function validates the input parameters
 * The system processes requests asynchronously
 * Users can configure settings through the UI
 * When enabled, it provides detailed logging information
 ```
 <!-- </example-bullet-punctuation> -->
 
 ## Code blocks and code spans
 
 * Use fenced code blocks consistently (prefer triple backticks) and surround them with a blank line before and after. Use fenced code instead of indented code blocks.
 * Always specify a language for fenced code blocks; use `text` if no highlighting is desired.
 * Avoid tabs; use spaces everywhere. Do not include hard tab characters in code, lists, or text.
 * Do not add spaces just inside backticks of code spans; write `` `code` `` not `` ` code ` ``.
 * For shell examples, do not prefix commands with `$` unless you also show the command output; prefer copy-pasteable commands without the prompt.
 * Use backticks for code fences consistently across the repository; do not use tildes.
 
 <!-- <example-code> -->
 ````markdown
 ```bash
 # Good
 echo "Hello"
 ```
 
 Some inline `code` here.
 ````
 <!-- </example-code> -->
 
 ## Links and images
 
 * Do not reverse link syntax; write `[text](url)`.
 * Do not use empty links like `[]()` or `(#)`; always provide a valid destination.
 * Avoid bare URLs; wrap them in angle brackets like `<https://example.com>` or make them proper links with text.
 * Ensure link fragments match generated heading IDs (kebab-case, lower-case). Use `<a id="...">` when needed.
 * Provide alternate text for all images. If an image must be hidden from assistive tech, use `aria-hidden="true"` in HTML.
 * Keep spaces out of link text brackets: `[text]`, not `[ text ]`.
 * Use a consistent link/image style within a document. Inline and autolink styles are allowed. When using full `[text][label]` or collapsed `[label][]` references, ensure the corresponding `[label]: URL` is defined. Remove unused or duplicate reference definitions.
 * If literal bracketed text is intended (not a link), escape the brackets as `\[text\]`.
 
 <!-- <example-links-images> -->
 ```markdown
 See <https://example.com> and [Docs](https://example.com/docs).
 
 ![Diagram](./diagram.png)
 ```
 <!-- </example-links-images> -->
 
 ## Spacing and blank lines
 
 * Limit paragraph and prose lines to approximately 500 characters; keep headings under 80 characters.
 * Do not add trailing spaces at the end of lines except when intentionally forcing a hard line break; when forcing breaks, use exactly two spaces.
 * Do not use multiple consecutive blank lines; keep at most one in a row.
 * Surround fenced code blocks, headings, lists, and tables with a blank line before and after (unless at file start/end).
 * Files must end with a single newline; no extra blank lines at EOF.
 * Do not break long URLs or long words to satisfy line length. Headings should honor their shorter limit; tables are exempt from line length checks. Code blocks may exceed normal line length; avoid wrapping code for width alone.
 
 ## Blockquotes
 
 * Use a single space after the `>` marker; avoid multiple spaces.
 * Do not place a bare blank line between adjacent blockquotes unless they are the same quote (then include `>` on the blank line to continue it).
 * Inside blockquotes, apply the same list and code rules; when creating tight lists with code fences inside blockquotes, consider whether a blank line is required for your target renderer.
 
 <!-- <example-blockquotes> -->
 ```markdown
 > Quoted text continues
 >
 > Same quote after a blank line.
 ```
 <!-- </example-blockquotes> -->
 
 ## Horizontal rules
 
 * Use one horizontal rule style consistently within a document. Prefer `---`.
 
 ## Emphasis
 
 * Use a consistent style for emphasis and strong emphasis throughout a document. Prefer `*italic*` and `**bold**` for new content.
 * Do not put spaces inside emphasis markers: `**bold**`, not `** bold **`.
 * Do not use emphasis-only lines as section separators; use proper headings instead.
  * Avoid emphasis within words using underscores; prefer asterisks for word-internal emphasis if absolutely necessary.
 
 ## Tables
 
 * Surround tables with a blank line before and after (unless at file start/end).
 * Use a consistent pipe style; prefer leading and trailing pipes on all rows.
 * Ensure every row has the same number of cells as the header.
 * Keep header and delimiter rows aligned in column count so the table is recognized by renderers.
 * Use aligned column style: all pipe characters must align vertically across all rows. Pad cell content with spaces so pipes line up.
 
 <!-- <example-tables> -->
 ```markdown
 | Column A | Column B | Column C |
 |----------|----------|----------|
 | Short    | Medium   | Longer   |
 | A        | BB       | CCC      |
 ```
 <!-- </example-tables> -->
 
 ## Miscellaneous
 
 * Do not include inline HTML unless necessary; if used, limit to explicitly allowed elements like `<details>` and `<summary>` in this repository.
 * Fenced code blocks must declare a language; use a recognized language name. If no highlighting is desired, use `text`.
 * Follow proper capitalization for product and technology names used in this repository (e.g., "GitHub", "JavaScript").
  * Avoid using inline HTML when a Markdown equivalent exists. If an inline HTML element is necessary and allowed, keep it minimal and well-formed.
 * Ensure files end with exactly one trailing newline character.
 * Use a consistent fence marker for code blocks (backticks) across a file.
 * Use a consistent emphasis style throughout a file (prefer asterisks for both italic and bold).
 * Validate intra-document link fragments; they must match the generated IDs of headings or explicitly provided anchors. Prefer lower-case, dash-separated fragments.
 * When using reference-style links or images, ensure the referenced labels are defined. Remove any unused or duplicate reference definitions. Keep the special checkbox syntax `[x]` intact.
 * Link and image styles allowed: autolinks `<https://...>`, inline `[text](url)`, and reference `[text][label]`/`[label][]`. Avoid bare URLs in text; prefer autolink syntax. Avoid inline links where the link text equals the same absolute URL with no title; prefer autolink.
 * For tables, apply a consistent leading/trailing pipe style; prefer both leading and trailing pipes. Ensure all rows have the same number of cells as the header.

 # Writing Style Instructions
 
 These instructions define writing style, voice, and tone conventions for markdown content. Apply these conventions to maintain consistency and authenticity across documentation.
 
 ## Voice and Tone
 
 Writing voice adapts to context while maintaining professionalism:
 
 * Maintain a clear, professional voice while adjusting formality to suit context
 * Write with authority while remaining accessible (expert without condescension)
 * Adapt tone and structure to match purpose and audience
 * Preserve clarity regardless of complexity
 
 For community-facing communication patterns, follow the guidelines in `community-interaction.instructions.md`.
 
 ### Formal Contexts
 
 Use these conventions for strategic documents, architecture decisions, and official communications:
 
 * Write in an authoritative yet accessible style
 * Use structured sections with precise vocabulary
 * Employ inclusive pronouns ("we", "our") to speak for the team
 * Maintain professionalism while remaining approachable
 
 ### Instructional Contexts
 
 Use these conventions for guides, tutorials, how-tos, and developer-facing content:
 
 * Adopt a warmer, more direct tone
 * Address the reader as "you" to create engagement
 * Use first-person reflections ("I") when sharing rationale or experience
 * Keep guidance actionable and concrete
 
 ## Language and Vocabulary
 
 Vocabulary choices affect clarity and reader engagement:
 
 * Use rich, varied vocabulary to avoid repetitive word choices within close proximity
 * Choose precise terms over vague alternatives; prefer specificity
 * Match vocabulary complexity to the audience without sacrificing accuracy
 * Avoid jargon unless the audience expects it; define terms when introducing them
 
 ## Sentence Structure
 
 Sentence variety improves readability:
 
 * Vary sentence length deliberately
 * Use longer, more complex sentences for narrative explanations and context-setting
 * Use shorter, punchy sentences for step-by-step instructions and emphasis
 * Maintain clarity regardless of sentence complexity
 * Avoid run-on sentences; break complex ideas into digestible parts
 * Use parallel structure in lists and comparisons
 
 ## Patterns to Avoid
 
 Avoid these common patterns that reduce clarity and create clutter.
 
 ### Em Dashes
 
 <!-- markdownlint-disable-next-line search-replace -->
 Do not use em dashes (—) for parenthetical statements, explanations, or dramatic pauses. Use these alternatives instead:
 
 | Instead of Em Dash  | Use This    | Example                                         |
 |---------------------|-------------|-------------------------------------------------|
 | Parenthetical aside | Commas      | "The system, when enabled, logs all events."    |
 | Explanation         | Colons      | "One option remains: refactor the module."      |
 | Emphasis            | Periods     | Create a new sentence when emphasizing a point. |
 | Supplementary info  | Parentheses | Use for truly supplementary information.        |
 
 ### Bolded-Prefix List Items
 
 Do not format lists with bolded terms followed by descriptions.
 
 ```markdown
 <!-- Avoid this pattern -->
 * **Configuration**: Set up the environment variables
 * **Deployment**: Push to production
 
 <!-- Use this pattern instead -->
 * Set up environment variables for configuration
 * Push to production for deployment
 ```
 
 Use plain lists, proper headings, or description lists instead.
 
 ### Hedging and Filler
 
 Remove these phrases that add no value:
 
 * "It's worth noting that..." (delete, state directly)
 * "It should be mentioned..." (delete, state directly)
 * "simply", "easily", "just" (delete)
 * "robust", "powerful", "seamless" (use specific descriptions)
 
 ### Self-Referential Writing
 
 Avoid meta-commentary about the document itself. Start with the content directly instead of phrases like "This document explains..." or "This page will show you..."
 
 ## Structural Patterns
 
 Organize content to help readers find and understand information:
 
 * Use structured sections with clear headings to organize content logically
 * Lead with context before diving into details
 * Group related information together
 * Provide transitions between major sections when helpful
 
 ## Callouts and Alerts
 
 Use GitHub-flavored markdown alerts for important callouts. Each alert type serves a specific purpose:
 
 | Alert          | Purpose                                                     |
 |----------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|
 | `[!NOTE]`      | Useful information users should know when skimming          |
 | `[!TIP]`       | Helpful advice for doing things better or more easily       |
 | `[!IMPORTANT]` | Key information users need to achieve their goal            |
 | `[!WARNING]`   | Urgent info needing immediate attention to avoid problems   |
 | `[!CAUTION]`   | Advises about risks or negative outcomes of certain actions |
 
 ```markdown
 > [!NOTE]
 > Useful information that users should know, even when skimming content.
 
 > [!TIP]
 > Helpful advice for doing things better or more easily.
 
 > [!IMPORTANT]
 > Key information users need to know to achieve their goal.
 
 > [!WARNING]
 > Urgent info that needs immediate user attention to avoid problems.
 
 > [!CAUTION]
 > Advises about risks or negative outcomes of certain actions.
 ```
 
 ## Pronoun Usage
 
 Match pronouns to context and purpose:
 
 | Context                    | Preferred Pronouns       | Example                                                          |
 |----------------------------|--------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
 | Team/organizational voice  | "we", "our"              | "We recommend using..."                                          |
 | Instructional/tutorial     | "you", "your"            | "You can configure..."                                           |
 | Personal insight/rationale | "I"                      | "I prefer this approach because..."                              |
 | Neutral/technical          | Impersonal constructions | "This configuration enables..."                                  |
 | Community interaction      | "we", "you"              | "Thank you for reporting this. We'll investigate and follow up." |
 
 ## Clarity Principles
 
 Clarity takes priority while balancing brevity:
 
 * Prioritize clarity over brevity, but aim for both when possible
 * Ensure complex ideas remain understandable through structure and word choice
 * Use examples to illustrate abstract concepts
 * Front-load important information; do not bury the lede
 
 ## Adaptability
 
 Adaptability is the hallmark of effective writing style. Shift register based on content purpose:
 
 | Formality Level | Use For                                                          | Characteristics                    |
 |-----------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
 | High            | Strategic plans, executive summaries, architecture decisions     | Structured, precise, authoritative |
 | Medium          | Technical documentation, READMEs, contributing guides            | Clear, professional, balanced      |
 | Lower           | Internal notes, casual updates, quick references                 | Direct, concise, conversational    |
 | Community       | Issue/PR comments, contributor acknowledgments, closure messages | Warm, appreciative, scope-focused  |
 
 Regardless of formality level, maintain professionalism and precision.

 ## Confirmed scope decisions
 
 * **Local-first demo.** The working demonstration runs locally on Podman. The MVP is complete at Phase 6.
 * **Cloud is conceptual plus IaC.** The Azure architecture (APIM, VNet, private endpoints, managed identity) exists to show the intended security posture. The full stack is not deployed, because APIM, AI Search, and private networking carry significant monthly cost.
 * **Network slice.** A separately deployable subset of the IaC (VNet, subnets, NSGs, egress, private DNS, and low-cost private-endpoint services) is designed in Phase 7. Deploying it needs the user and is not required for the demo.
 * **Models.** Chat and embedding models are Microsoft Foundry deployments supplied by the user: chat `gpt-5` and embeddings `text-embedding-3-small` (1,536 dimensions), both verified reachable on 2026-11-22.  * **Search.** Local and cloud both use the user-provided Azure AI Search service. There is no local vector store (no PostgreSQL/pgvector), which removes the local-versus-cloud adapter mismatch. The local demo therefore depends on network access to Azure.
 * **IaC modules.** Use pinned Azure Verified Modules (AVM) where available, with thin composition modules otherwise.

 Deliver a demonstrable support assistant that answers questions about a documented, explicitly selected set of 100 OpenText products. Responses must be grounded in anonymously accessible source material, cite the source URL for each product or resource claim, and clearly disclose the limited demo catalog. The architecture should provide a safe path to later customer validation and production without representing the MVP as a production service.
 
 The longer-term OpenText Service Management expansion is an architectural consideration, not MVP scope.
 
 The demo runs locally. The Azure design is presented as a validated blueprint, with an explicit statement of which security controls are demonstrated locally and which are designed only.

 ## Target architecture to validate
 
 The proposed flow is:
 
 1. A one-time catalog process obtains the product list, selects and records a stable 100-product demo manifest, and publishes one product reference per queue message.
 2. A scheduled, resumable documentation ingestion job reads a versioned source map of approved seeds. It fetches only allowlisted, `robots.txt`-permitted public URLs, observes HTTP status and retry headers, and skips authentication-protected material. It records durable per-URL fetch state, then normalizes and chunks permitted content, creates embeddings through a gateway, and updates the search index idempotently ([ADR-0006](./architecture/decisions/adr-0006-periodic-resumable-source-ingestion.md)).
 3. A coverage API derives a per-product status from the manifest, source map, and fetch state. The UI discloses which products are covered.
 4. The retrieval layer combines keyword, metadata, and semantic signals and returns source IDs, URLs, and relevant excerpts with each result.
 5. A FastAPI service coordinates retrieval and a Microsoft Agent Framework agent. A model gateway provides a replaceable interface for embedding and chat models.
 6. A React/Next.js frontend provides the user-facing chat experience, clearly identifies the demo catalog, and renders citations supplied by retrieval rather than invented by the model.
 7. OpenTelemetry-compatible traces, metrics, and appropriately minimized logs support evaluation and operations. Production cloud resources use managed identity where supported; GitHub Actions uses federated identity for deployment.
 
 The [architecture overview](./architecture/architecture-overview.md) contains the current context, container, ingestion process, resume, coverage, planned chat, data ownership, trust boundary, and deployment diagrams.

 1. **Containers.** Add `Containerfile`s for the API and web app, and add `api` and `web` services to `compose.yaml`, loopback-bound, with health checks. Add the LiteLLM service if Phase 4 step 7 was done. Ingestion stays a one-shot `podman compose run` job.
 2. **Evaluation set (closes D3-3 in demo form).** Add `tests/evaluation/questions-v1.json` with about 15 questions across the 10 covered products, each with the expected product ID and at least one expected `source_url`, plus 3 unanswerable questions. Add `scripts/run_evaluation.py`, which runs the questions through the API. It reports top-five retrieval hit rate (target ≥ 80% for the demo), citation validity (target 100% of citations resolve to retrieved evidence), and refusal on unanswerable questions (target 3 of 3). Write the results to `docs/operations/phase-6-evaluation-v1.md`.
 3. **Semantic reranking.** If the Search tier supports semantic ranker, run the evaluation with and without it and record the choice. Otherwise record "not available on this tier".
 4. **Runbook.** Update [local development](./operations/local-development.md) with prerequisites, `.env` keys, start order, ingest, index, chat, evaluation, and teardown.
 5. **Logging.** Add request ID, latency, token counts, and outcome to the logs, with no query or response text. OpenTelemetry export is optional.
 
 **Exit criteria:** On a clean checkout with `.env` filled, the runbook brings up the demo, a question returns a cited answer, the evaluation meets its demo targets, and all routine checks pass.
 
 **Production-only (recorded, not done here):** human-reviewed evaluation set and thresholds, latency and cost SLOs, OpenTelemetry to Azure Monitor, a red-team suite in CI, retention policy approval, and a MongoDB snapshot or restore procedure.
 
 ### Phase 7: Cloud architecture, IaC, and CI/CD definitions
 
 **Status:** Can run in parallel with Phases 4 to 6. Demo delivery mode covers authoring and static validation. Deploying anything to Azure still needs the user ([ADR-0007](./architecture/decisions/adr-0007-demo-delivery-mode.md)).
 
 **Goal:** Show the intended Azure architecture as validated Bicep, plus GitHub Actions pipelines for IaC and for application build and deployment.
 
 **Work packages:**
 
 1. **Bicep (`infra/bicep/`).** Add a subscription-scope `main.bicep` that creates the resource group, and modules for:
    * Network: VNet, subnets for Container Apps and private endpoints, NSGs, and NAT Gateway.
    * Platform services: Log Analytics, Application Insights, Key Vault, and ACR.
    * A Container Apps environment with `api` and `web` apps and a scheduled ingestion job (cron, weekly).
    * Cosmos DB for MongoDB, a Storage queue, and Azure AI Search, each with a private endpoint and a private DNS zone.
    * A user-assigned managed identity with least-privilege role assignments.
    * Foundry endpoint and deployment names as parameters. Never put secrets in parameters.
 
    Use pinned AVM modules where they fit (see `.github/agents/azure-verified-modules-bicep.agent.md` and `.github/instructions/bicep-code-best-practices.instructions.md`). Add `parameters/dev.bicepparam` and a `bicepconfig.json`. APIM is optional: include it as a module behind a `deployApim` boolean, default `false`, because of its cost.
 2. **Naming and tags.** Add a short table in `infra/README.md` with the pattern `{type}-psa-{env}-cac-{nn}` and the mandatory tags.
 3. **IaC pipeline (`.github/workflows/infra.yml`).** On a pull request to `infra/**`, run `bicep build`, `bicep lint`, and `az deployment sub what-if` (what-if needs OIDC secrets; skip it when they are absent).  4. **App pipeline (`.github/workflows/app.yml`).** Run the Python and web checks, build the container images, and push to ACR on `main`. Deploy to Container Apps on `workflow_dispatch` with the `dev` environment.
 5. **Pinning.** Pin all actions by full SHA (follow `.github/instructions/ci-security.instructions.md`). Use `permissions: contents: read` by default, with `id-token: write` only on jobs that need it.
 6. **Bootstrap doc.** Document the one-time Entra app registration and federated credentials in `infra/README.md`.
 
 **Exit criteria:** `bicep build` and `bicep lint` pass locally. `actionlint` passes on all workflows. `what-if` runs if the subscription is available; otherwise record that it was skipped. The architecture overview's deployment diagram matches the Bicep.
 
 **Production-only (recorded, not done here):** PSRule or Checkov policy gates, the custom structural checks (CIDR overlap, DNS pairing), actual network-slice deployment and teardown, a detailed cost estimate, APIM SKU selection, and branch protection with required reviewers.
 
 ### Phase 8: Cloud deployment and pilot (not in demo scope)
 
 Deploying the application stack to Azure and running a pilot requires the user. It needs a budget, a chosen APIM SKU, and the production-only items from Phases 4 to 7. The Phase 7 pipelines make it a `workflow_dispatch` away once approved.

 **Goal:** One page that lists what separates the demo from production.

 | Boundary | Crossing data or action | Main concern |

 | TB-07 Services to telemetry | Operational events; optionally retained content only after approval | Secret/content leakage and excessive access |
 | TB-08 Developer machine to user-provided services | Authentication tokens, keys, configuration | Local credential exposure and unintended service access |
 | TB-09 Cloud application boundary, design-only | APIM, Container Apps, managed identities, private services | Incorrect network, identity, or policy assumptions |

 ## Source verification
 
 The initial probe used three GETs. After additional budget approval, one more
 GET was used to read a bounded feed prefix. Redirects were not followed, and no
 response body was stored.
 
 | Endpoint | Result | Interpretation |
 |---|---|---|
 | [Product listing](https://my.opentext.com/support/products/) | HTTP 200, `text/html`; 3,105 bytes inspected, with no anchor or script tags in the inspected prefix | A successful HTTP status did not establish that the response contains the product catalog. Server-rendering and page semantics remain unverified. |
 | [Search results API](https://my.opentext.com/api/web/support/search-results?start=1&maxResults=5&text=%2A) | HTTP 401, `text/plain` | Treat this API response as protected. Do not retry with credentials or treat it as an empty catalog. |
 | [Product feed](https://my.opentext.com/api/web/feed/product) | HTTP 200, `application/json`; an additional bounded read reached 16,385 bytes and was truncated | The complete feed was not downloaded or parsed. The response is larger than the probe limit; pagination, size, and parsing remain unverified. No response body was retained. |
 
 The initial probe used three GETs. Of the original 100 additional GETs, one was
 previously used for a bounded feed-prefix read. The live verification used two
 feed GETs and 97 product-page GETs, exhausting that original additional budget.
 The user separately authorized one full-feed GET, which was also used in this
 verification. This accounts for 100 GETs under the original additional cap plus
 one separately authorized full-feed GET; the cumulative count including the
 initial three probes is 104.
 
 The full feed parsed into 1,302 unique products and produced the
 [100-product manifest](../operations/phase-2-product-manifest-v1.json). Of the
 97 product pages checked, all returned HTTP 200 but the login-content heuristic
 classified them as protected. Three manifest products were not checked. Since
 response bodies were not retained, those classifications are inconclusive. The
 [outcome report](../operations/phase-2-ingestion-outcome-v1.md) records the
 details. No page content was stored, and the live check did not enqueue products
 or persist ingestion run records. The user approved Phase 2 on 2026-11-21.
 
 On 2026-11-22, a separately authorized check issued 100 anonymous GETs, one to
 each manifest product page. All returned HTTP 200 and were classified by the
 login-content heuristic as protected. No bodies were retained, so these
 classifications remain inconclusive. The [metadata-only report](../operations/phase-3-source-check-2026-11-22.json)
 records each outcome.
 
 The user then authorized further anonymous checks until ten products with
 usable content are found. In 172 GETs across two bounded batches, the follow-up
 review checked all 100 manifest product pages and inspected the public feed and
 client assets. Product detail is client-rendered; the raw HTML did not establish
 product-specific content, and request-capped browser checks were inconclusive.
 The feed contains nonempty descriptions for four manifest products, without a
 review of their suitability. Most documentation links use hosts outside the
 current allowlist; none of those hosts was contacted. The
 [follow-up report](../operations/phase-3-anonymous-source-review-2026-11-22.json)
 contains request metadata and no response bodies.
 
 On 2026-11-22, the [delivery probe](../operations/phase-3-source-delivery-probe-2026-11-22.json)
 used about 35 anonymous GETs to establish how the observed documentation is
 delivered. The `docs.microfocus.com` portal serves its table of contents and
 page bodies as anonymous JSON. The `admhelp.microfocus.com` help sites serve
 server-rendered HTML and publish per-product sitemaps. The `robots.txt` files on
 both hosts allow the selected paths. One end-to-end page fetch returned real
 text. Fortify SAST returned HTTP 403 and was excluded. Bodies were inspected
 only to identify the formats and were not retained.
 
 ## Proposed manifest and ingestion contract
 
 * Generate a manifest only from a successfully parsed and deduplicated catalog.
 * Store a manifest version, selection method, selected product identifiers,
   display names, canonical product URLs, and selection timestamp.
 * Reuse the same manifest for normal reruns. Replacing the sample requires an
   explicit operation and a new version.
 * Enqueue one product reference per message. Never place source content or
   credentials in queue messages.
 * Use stable source/document/chunk identifiers and content hashes for
   idempotency. Record product-level success, protected skip, retry, and failure
   outcomes without retaining protected content.
 * Treat changes to source content, parser version, embedding deployment, and
   embedding dimensions as index-versioning events.
 * Define retry, poison-message, deletion, stale-content, and partial-run behavior
   before Phase 2 implementation.
 
 ## Phase 0 exit review
 
 The user approved the proposed Phase 0 direction with amendments and authorized
 Phase 0b. The live feed is parsed and a manifest is available. The product
 pages turned out to be client-rendered and are now the catalog only (see
 [ADR-0006](decisions/adr-0006-periodic-resumable-source-ingestion.md)). The
 user approved Phase 2 on 2026-11-21 and Phase 3 on 2026-11-22. No further
 source request is authorized without explicit approval. The original
 additional GET budget is exhausted; source approval does not bypass later phase
 gates.
 
 The full phase gate is listed in the
 [implementation plan](../implementation-plan.md#phase-0-product-discovery-and-architecture-decisions).

 ## Status
 
 Accepted by the user on 2026-11-22. This ADR supersedes the per-phase approval
 loop described in earlier versions of the
 [implementation plan](../../implementation-plan.md).
 
 ## Context
 
 The goal is a working local demo that runs end to end against real Azure
 resources (Microsoft Foundry models and Azure AI Search). The demo is followed
 by CI/CD definitions for IaC and for build and deployment. The demo exists to
 show web and agentic architecture skills. It is not meant to be a
 production-ready application.
 
 The earlier plan required explicit approval before every phase, every live
 request batch, and every exit item. That loop cost more time than the risk it
 controlled. Phases stalled on approvals that matter only before a production
 release.
 
 ## Decision
 
 ### Delivery mode
 
 The project runs in **demo delivery mode** until a production decision is
 made. In this mode, a contributor, human or coding agent, may proceed through
 Phases 4 to 7 without asking for approval, as long as the guardrails below hold.
 
 ### Guardrails that always apply
 
 These are cheap, protect real systems, and stay in force in demo mode:
 
 1. Never commit secrets, `.env`, scraped content, or MongoDB data.
 2. Anonymous access only. Never authenticate to, or bypass, a protected source.
 3. Fetch source content only from the versioned
    [source map](../../operations/phase-3-source-map-v1.json), through the
    source worker, which enforces `robots.txt`, request budgets, and backoff.
 4. Keep citations bound to retrieved evidence. The model never authors URLs.
 5. Keep query/response retention off (`QUERY_RESPONSE_RETENTION_ENABLED=false`).
 6. Bind local services to loopback. Do not expose the demo publicly.
 7. Keep routine tests offline (fakes and mocks). Live tests are opt-in with
    `-m live`.
 8. Keep `ruff`, `mypy`, `pytest`, `bandit`, and the web checks passing.
 
 ### Pre-authorized actions
 
 Actions authorized for the demo without further approval:
 
 | Action | Limit |
 |---|---|
 | Live documentation ingestion with `scripts/run_source_ingestion.py` | The default budget (400 requests per run), at most one run per day; a weekly schedule is fine |
 | Calls to the user-provided Foundry chat and embedding deployments in `.env` | Demo and test traffic only; keep batches small |
 | Creating, updating, or deleting indexes in the user-provided Azure AI Search service | Index names must start with `product-support-` |
 | Live integration tests against a `product-support-test-*` index | Opt-in with `pytest -m live` |
 | Local Podman containers for this project | The project's `compose.yaml` services only; do not touch other projects' containers |
 | Authoring Bicep, GitHub Actions workflows, and pipeline definitions | Authoring and static validation (`az bicep build`, `what-if` where possible) |
 
 ### Actions that still need the user
 
 * Creating or changing Azure resources other than the Search indexes above,
   including deploying the network slice or the application.
 * Spending outside the existing deployments, such as new model deployments or
   SKU changes.
 * Adding a new source host or product to the source map.
 * Enabling query/response retention.
 
 ### Deferred to production
 
 The following controls are part of a production-grade delivery. They are
 **recorded and designed, not performed** for the demo, and do not block any
 demo phase:
 
 | Area | Production expectation | Demo treatment |
 |---|---|---|
 | Phase gates | Formal exit review and sign-off per phase | Exit criteria are the definition of done; no sign-off loop |
 | Source terms | Legal review of documentation reuse terms | Public, `robots.txt`-permitted docs used for a private, non-commercial demo; review before any public or commercial use |
 | Retrieval quality | Reviewed, versioned relevance set with agreed thresholds and sign-off | Small synthetic evaluation set with the documented thresholds (Phase 6); no human review panel |
 | Semantic reranking | Measured decision against the reviewed set | Off by default; may be enabled if the Search tier allows it, noted in the plan |
 | Usability | Moderated study with representative users | Self-walkthrough of the five demo tasks |
 | Accessibility | Automated scans plus manual keyboard and screen-reader review against WCAG 2.2 AA | Semantic HTML, labels, and keyboard checks; a full audit is deferred |
 | Privacy | Approved notice, reviewer access, redaction, TTL, and deletion before retention | Retention stays off |
 | Threat model | Every high-rated threat tested or formally accepted per phase | Register maintained; tests for the guardrails above; remaining threats noted as production work |
 | Identity | Entra ID, managed identity, and keyless access to Search and Foundry | API keys from `.env` |
 | Network | Private endpoints, VNet, and controlled egress | Public endpoints from the developer machine |
 | Observability | OpenTelemetry to Azure Monitor with retention policy | Structured, redacted logs; optional local tracing |
 | Supply chain | Branch protection, required checks, image scanning, provenance | CI workflow runs checks; branch protection is a backlog item |
 | Operations | SLOs, on-call, incident response, backup and restore | Not applicable to a local demo |
 
 ## Consequences
 
 * Phases 4 to 7 can be completed in sequence without waiting for approvals,
   within the guardrails and pre-authorized actions.
 * The documentation still shows the production path: each deferred control has
   a design or an entry in the threat register, the security posture, or the
   production gap register (Phase 9).
 * Any move toward production, a public demo, or customer data reopens the
   deferred controls. They then become blocking.
 
 ## Alternatives considered
 
 * Keep per-phase approval: rejected, because it was the main delay and
   protected nothing that mattered for a private demo.
 * Drop the governance documentation entirely: rejected, because the
   documentation shows that the production controls are understood.

 title: Local Development Runbook
 description: Run the product support demo locally with Podman Compose
 author: Product Support Agent Team
 ms.date: 2026-11-22
 ms.topic: how-to
 keywords:
   - local development
   - Podman
   - Next.js
   - FastAPI
 ---
 
 # Local development
 
 This runbook starts the local demo against the existing Microsoft Foundry and
 Azure AI Search services. The browser talks only to Next.js; Next.js calls
 FastAPI over the Compose network. No query or response history is stored.
 
 ## Prerequisites and environment
 
 * Podman with a running machine and a working `podman compose` provider.
 * Network access to the user's Foundry and Azure AI Search endpoints.
 * Valid deployment and Search credentials in a local `.env` file.
 * `uv` 0.13.9 or later for running the evaluation and Python checks.
 
 From a clean checkout, copy `.env.example` once, then fill in the existing
 deployment and Search values locally. Do not overwrite an existing `.env`:
 
 ```powershell
 if (-not (Test-Path .env)) { Copy-Item .env.example .env }
 ```
 
 Required settings in `.env` are:
 
 * `AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT` (OpenAI-compatible endpoint ending in `/openai/v1`),
   `AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY`, and `AZURE_OPENAI_CHAT_DEPLOYMENT`.
 * `AZURE_OPENAI_EMBEDDING_ENDPOINT` and
   `AZURE_OPENAI_EMBEDDING_DEPLOYMENT`.
 * `AZURE_AI_SEARCH_ENDPOINT` and `AZURE_AI_SEARCH_API_KEY`.
 * `PRODUCT_SUPPORT_SEARCH_EMBEDDING_MODEL_VERSION`,
   `PRODUCT_SUPPORT_SEARCH_EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS` (`1536`), and
   `PRODUCT_SUPPORT_SEARCH_DEMO_INDEX_BASE` (`product-support-demo`).
 * `PRODUCT_SUPPORT_MONGODB_URI` may remain
   `mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017` in the host `.env`; Compose overrides it inside
   the API container with `mongodb://mongodb:27017`.
 
 Leave `CHAT_TEMPERATURE` empty. The gpt-5 chat deployment rejects a temperature
 parameter, so the chat client omits it. Query/response retention must remain
 disabled.
 
 Compose passes `.env` only to the API service using `env_file`; secrets are not
 baked into either image. The web service receives only
 `PRODUCT_SUPPORT_API_BASE_URL=http://api:8000`. The API image contains the
 approved manifest and source map JSON files, not the rest of `docs/`.
 
 ## Start the demo
 
 Start the Podman machine only if it is stopped:
 
 ```powershell
 podman machine list
 # If it is not running:
 podman machine start
 ```
 
 From the repository root, one command builds and starts MongoDB, Azurite, the
 API, and the web app. Health checks gate startup order, and published ports bind
 only to loopback:
 
 ```powershell
 podman compose up --build -d
 ```
 
 Open `http://127.0.0.1:3000`. The coverage page reports the 100-product
 manifest, the 10 products with approved public sources, and the current
 indexed-page count. The API health endpoint is `http://127.0.0.1:8000/healthz`;
 coverage metadata is at `http://127.0.0.1:8000/catalog/coverage`. The browser
 does not call FastAPI directly.
 
 The checked-in local database volume may already contain the 300 canonical
 pages ingested for the 10 covered products. A new empty MongoDB volume needs a
 bounded ingestion and indexing pass before chat can answer:
 
 ```powershell
 podman compose run --rm api uv run --no-sync python scripts/run_source_ingestion.py
 podman compose run --rm api uv run --no-sync python scripts/index_documents.py
 ```
 
 Ingestion uses only
 [`phase-3-source-map-v1.json`](./phase-3-source-map-v1.json), the configured
 request budget, robots policy, freshness checks, and backoff. Indexing creates
 or updates the `product-support-demo-*` Search index from canonical MongoDB
 documents using the Foundry embedding deployment. These commands do not
 provision Azure resources. Rerun indexing after ingesting new or changed pages.
 
 Ask a question in the web page and optionally filter to an indexed product.
 Answers are plain text; citation links come from retrieved evidence. If no
 indexed evidence answers a question, the UI shows
 “No indexed documentation answers this.” Do not assume products without an
 approved source are supported.
 
 ## Evaluation
 
 The versioned set contains 15 answerable questions across the 10 covered
 products and 3 unanswerable questions. The runner queries hybrid retrieval and
 the local API, then writes metrics and per-case outcomes only; it does not
 write question or response text to the report.
 
 ```powershell
 uv sync --all-groups
 uv run python scripts/run_evaluation.py --api-url http://127.0.0.1:8000
 ```
 
 Results are recorded in
 [`phase-6-evaluation-v1.md`](./phase-6-evaluation-v1.md). Semantic reranking
 was not enabled because the Search service tier and billing plan could not be
 verified; no service setting was changed.
 
 ## Stop and preserve local data
 
 Stop the containers gracefully while keeping the named data volumes:
 
 ```powershell
 podman compose stop --timeout 30
 ```
 
 Restart them with `podman compose start`. To remove project containers while
 preserving data, use `podman compose down --timeout 30`. Do not add `--volumes`
 unless you intentionally want to delete the MongoDB and Azurite data. Leave
 containers from other projects alone.
 
 ## Routine validation
 
 From the repository root:
 
 ```powershell
 uv run ruff format --check .
 uv run ruff check .
 uv run mypy src/product_support_agent scripts
 uv run pytest
 uv run bandit -q -r src scripts
 ```
 
 In `apps/web`:
 
 ```powershell
 npm run lint
 npm run typecheck
 npm run build
 ```
 
 ## Production-only
 
 This runbook is for a local demo, not a public or production service. Identity,
 private networking, rate and cost controls, reviewed evaluation, full
 accessibility and red-team audits, query/response retention approval,
 observability export, image provenance, and MongoDB backup/restore remain
 documented gaps in the
 [production gap register](./production-gap-register.md).

 author: Product Support Agent Team

 # Production readiness gap register
 
 ## Intentional demo scope
 
 The controls below are known and documented. This iteration prioritized a
 working local system over production readiness; their absence is an intentional
 demo-scope decision, not an untracked omission. Completing this register does
 not approve a public or production launch.
 
 The register consolidates the deferred controls in
 [ADR-0007](../architecture/decisions/adr-0007-demo-delivery-mode.md), the
 Phase 4–7 **Production-only** notes in the
 [implementation plan](../implementation-plan.md), open items in the
 [threat register](../security/threat-register.md), and risks in the
 [risk-and-assumption register](../architecture/risk-assumptions.md).
 
 | Gap | Owner role | Blocking trigger | Demo treatment and production work |
 |---|---|---|---|
 | Source terms and reuse rights (R-09) | Product owner / legal | Public or commercial use of indexed content | The demo uses only the approved source map and anonymous access. Review and record reuse terms before expanding beyond this private demo. |
 | Retrieval quality and evaluation (D3-3, R-11) | Search and support-content owners | Customer-facing answers or a quality commitment | The 15-question evaluation reached 80% expected-source hits in the top five, 28/28 citation URL matches, and 3/3 unanswerable refusals. The set is small and not human-reviewed; broaden and approve the set and thresholds before launch. |
 | Semantic reranking | Search owner | Relevance improvement is required or before a production ranking decision | Not evaluated: the Search service tier and billing plan could not be verified. No setting was changed; confirm availability and billing before testing it. |
 | Prompt injection and model-output links (T-01, T-05, T-16, R-06) | Agent and application-security owners | Public exposure or reliance on answers for customer action | Retrieved text is treated as untrusted; citations are evidence-bound, model-authored URLs are removed, and focused prompt-injection and citation-forgery cases pass. Add independent red-team coverage and review output-safety controls. |
 | Chat abuse and spend controls (T-08, R-05) | AI platform owner | Public access, shared usage, or a committed cost limit | `/chat` bounds message size, tool calls, concurrency, and elapsed time. Global rate limits, per-user budgets, quota alerts, and cost SLOs are production work. |
 | Authentication and least privilege (T-11, T-14) | Identity and application owners | Public demo, customer data, or production launch | The application is anonymous and loopback-bound; local service keys come from `.env`. Add user authentication and managed identity or equivalent least-privilege access before broader exposure. |
 | Private networking and egress (T-15, R-07) | Cloud/network architect | Production deployment or access to private data | The local demo reaches user-provided public Foundry and Search endpoints. Validate private endpoints, DNS, service tiers, quota, and allowlisted egress in the cloud design before deployment. |
 | Query/response privacy and retention (R-04) | Privacy owner | Any request to retain user content or process customer data | Retention remains off and query/response text is not logged. Approve notice, provider handling, reviewer access, redaction, TTL, and deletion before enabling retention. |
 | Observability and service objectives | Operations and security owners | Production launch or a support commitment | Logs carry request IDs, latency, token counts, and outcomes without query/response text. Define latency/cost SLOs, alerting, trace controls, and Azure Monitor export. |
 | Usability and accessibility (R-08) | Product and accessibility owners | Public or customer-facing release | The demo has labels, keyboard operation, visible focus, `aria-live`, and a self-walkthrough. Conduct moderated usability and full WCAG 2.2 AA keyboard and screen-reader review. |
 | Supply-chain assurance (T-13) | Build and release owner | Publishing images or production deployment | Dependencies are locked and CI checks run; local container images build successfully. Add image scanning, SBOM/provenance, signing, protected release environments, and required branch checks. |
 | Backup, restore, and incident operations | Data and operations owners | Production launch or any non-recoverable data | MongoDB data is local and no snapshot/restore procedure, on-call rotation, or incident-response process is defined. Establish and test them before production use. |
 | Product and source coverage (R-11) | Product owner / ingestion lead | A broader product-support claim or a new source host/product | Only 10 of the 100 manifest products have approved sources. Keep the coverage disclosure; review new products or hosts before adding them. |
 | Azure application deployment | Cloud platform owner | Any Azure application workload or new Azure resource | The demo stack is local. Azure deployment, resource creation other than approved Search indexes, and new spend require separate user authorization. |
 
 ## Current release boundary
 
 The local demo is not approved for public access, customer data, or production
 operations. Keep services bound to `127.0.0.1`, use only the versioned
 source map, and keep query/response retention disabled.

 # Product Support Agent
 
 This repository contains a local-first product support assistant demo that runs
 against real Azure resources (Microsoft Foundry and Azure AI Search). It is built
 in **demo delivery mode** ([ADR-0007](docs/architecture/decisions/adr-0007-demo-delivery-mode.md)):
 it aims for a working demo and records production-only controls instead of
 blocking on them.
 The TypeScript React/Next.js frontend and Python FastAPI backend now provide a
 grounded chat demo. The browser talks only to Next.js; the server-side route
 calls FastAPI. Chat and embeddings use the user's Microsoft Foundry deployments
 directly through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and retrieval uses the user's
 Azure AI Search service. Search citations are resolved from retrieved evidence;
 the model cannot author their URLs.
 
 The approved source map covers 10 of the 100 manifest products. The resumable
 worker ([ADR-0006](docs/architecture/decisions/adr-0006-periodic-resumable-source-ingestion.md))
 stored 300 pages in MongoDB, and Phase 4 indexed 952 chunks into the demo Search
 index. The local Compose stack includes MongoDB, Azurite, FastAPI, and Next.js.
 The Phase 6 evaluation reached an 80% expected-source hit rate in the top five,
 100% citation URL matches, and 3/3 refusals for unanswerable questions; see the
 [evaluation report](docs/operations/phase-6-evaluation-v1.md).
 
 Phases 0 to 6 are complete. The [local runbook](docs/operations/local-development.md)
 starts the stack with `podman compose up --build -d`. This is a local demo, not
 a production deployment; see the [production gap register](docs/operations/production-gap-register.md)
 for deferred controls and their blocking triggers.
 
 See the [architecture overview](docs/architecture/architecture-overview.md) for
 the current process and component diagrams.
 
 See the [implementation plan](docs/implementation-plan.md) for phase status and
 the [local development guide](docs/operations/local-development.md) for setup

 * Each high-rated threat must have a mitigation and test owner before the phase

 re-rated.

Gitleaks runs in CI. | First GitHub-hosted Gitleaks run; trace and span redaction plus canary checks in Phase 6. Redaction is pattern-based, so query and response content must never be logged. |

 Delivered and verified offline (242 local tests; Ruff, mypy, and Bandit clean):

 The earlier source investigations are recorded in the

 Their "inconclusive" product-page classifications are resolved. Product pages
 are client-rendered and are used as the catalog only.
 
 Accepted deferrals and where they are now handled:
 
 | ID | Deferred exit item | Why deferred | Closed by |
 |---|---|---|---|
 | D3-1 | First live ingestion run | — | **Closed on 2026-11-22.** 302 of 400 requests; 300 pages for 10 products stored in MongoDB; 0 failures. The source-terms legal review moved to production-only (ADR-0007) |
 | D3-2 | Live integration tests against the Azure AI Search test index, plus embedding the demo corpus | Needs the embedder, now built and unit tested, and a run | Phase 4, work packages 1 and 2 |
 | D3-3 | Retrieval relevance evaluation and the semantic reranking decision | Needs indexed content | Phase 6, work packages 2 and 3, in demo form. A human-reviewed relevance set is production-only |
 
 **Goal:** Turn permitted source material into traceable, updateable search results.
 
 **Scope and deliverables:**
 
 * Define and version canonical document and chunk schemas, stable IDs, content hashes, provenance, and update/delete behavior.
 * Implement parsing and normalization for approved public source formats; reject unsupported or oversized content safely.
 * Define chunking, metadata filters, embedding model/version, and index schema.
 * Implement the Azure AI Search provider behind a thin retrieval/indexing interface, plus an in-memory fake used by routine unit tests. Create and version the index definition as code and apply it with a script or the SDK.
 * Implement hybrid keyword, metadata, and semantic retrieval with configurable ranking and return source IDs, URLs, and excerpts.
 * Add index reconciliation and reprocessing for changed/deleted source content.
 * Ingest only from a versioned source map of approved seeds (docs-portal TOC JSON or XML sitemaps), with separate fetch and citation URLs, `robots.txt` enforcement, and per-product page caps.
 * Make ingestion periodic and resumable. Durable per-URL fetch state skips successes from the last 24 hours, unchanged revisions, and unchanged bodies, and uses conditional GETs. Failures fail fast with classified backoff, and a single-runner lease prevents overlapping runs.
 
 **Verification and exit gate:**
 
 * Unit tests cover normalization, canonical identity, chunk provenance, schema evolution, and idempotent updates.
 * Unit tests cover robots matching, source map validation, discovery, restart and resume without refetching, lost-state recovery, fail-fast and backoff, host abort on rate limiting, request budgets, and deletion of pages that leave the selection.
 * Integration tests verify indexing, metadata filters, hybrid retrieval, source URL preservation, and deletion/reindex behavior. They run against a dedicated Azure AI Search test index as controlled live tests; routine unit tests use the in-memory fake, and CI does not require Azure Search unless approved.
 * A reviewed retrieval test set meets agreed relevance and citation-source thresholds against Azure AI Search, using a dedicated test index separate from the demo index.
 * You approve schema, freshness behavior, and retrieval quality before agent integration.
 
 **Depends on:** Phase 2 approval; Phase 0 data ownership and retrieval decisions.
 
 ### Phase 4: FastAPI and grounded agent orchestration
 
 **Status:** Complete (2026-11-22). Indexed the existing 300 canonical documents (952 chunks) into the demo index; the marked live Search test passed; three manual Foundry/Search questions returned grounded answers with retrieval-bound citations. The final live check returned HTTP 200 with three citations and logged token counts without query or response text. Targeted chat tests: 15 passed. Full checks passed: `uv run ruff format --check .`, `uv run ruff check .`, `uv run mypy src/product_support_agent scripts`, `uv run pytest` (310 passed, 1 deselected), `uv run bandit -q -r src scripts`, and in `apps/web`, `npm run lint`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm run build`.
 
 | Exit criterion | Result | Evidence |
 |---|---|---|
 | Live Search and Foundry chat return grounded answers with citations | Pass | Marked live Search test passed; three manual Foundry/Search questions returned retrieval-bound citations |
 | Fake-model tests cover validation, citation binding, no evidence, and provider errors | Pass | 15 targeted chat tests passed, including forged, unknown, and URL-injected IDs |
 | Retrieved prompt injection cannot author links or citations | Pass | Prompt-injection regression test passed with the injected link instruction |
 | Routine Python and web checks pass | Pass | Ruff format/check, mypy, pytest (310 passed, 1 deselected), Bandit, and web lint/typecheck/build passed |
 
 **Goal:** Answer product-support questions over the indexed documentation, using structured tool calling, with citations the model cannot forge.
 
 **Starting point (already in the repository):**
 
 * `OpenAICompatibleEmbedder` in `embeddings.py`, tested. It calls Foundry today and LiteLLM later; only the base URL changes.
 * `ModelAndSearchSettings` in `config.py`. It reads the `AZURE_OPENAI_*`, `AZURE_AI_SEARCH_*`, and `PRODUCT_SUPPORT_SEARCH_*` variables already in `.env`.
 * `scripts/index_documents.py`, which embeds the canonical chunks from MongoDB into a versioned `product-support-demo-*` index. It has not been run yet.
 * `AzureAISearchProvider.search` (hybrid) and `InMemorySearchProvider` for tests.
 * `GET /catalog/coverage`, the source of the covered product IDs.
 
 **Work packages (in order):**
 
 1. **Index the demo corpus.** Run `uv run python scripts/run_source_ingestion.py`; it skips anything fetched in the last 24 hours. Then run `uv run python scripts/index_documents.py`. Record the index name and document count in [local development](./operations/local-development.md). This closes D3-1 and the indexing part of D3-2.
 2. **Live Search integration tests (closes D3-2).** Add `tests/integration/test_live_search.py`, marked `@pytest.mark.live` and skipped unless `-m live` is passed. Use a `product-support-test-*` index with 3 to 5 synthetic documents. Check upsert, the product-ID filter, hybrid query results, preserved `source_url` and IDs, stale-chunk removal on re-upload, and deletion. Delete the index at the end. Register the `live` marker in `pyproject.toml` and exclude it by default.
 3. **Retrieval service.** Add a function that takes a question and optional product IDs, embeds the question with `embed_query`, calls `search`, and returns `SearchResult` items. Only covered products are searchable.
 4. **Agent.** Use Microsoft Agent Framework for Python (see `.github/skills/microsoft-agent-framework`), pinned in `pyproject.toml`. Expose one tool, `search_documentation(query, product_ids?)`, that returns evidence items `{evidence_id, title, excerpt, product_id}`. The URL is not included. The system prompt says: answer only from evidence; cite evidence IDs as `[E1]`; say so when nothing relevant was found; never output URLs. Chat goes to the Foundry chat deployment (`AZURE_OPENAI_CHAT_DEPLOYMENT`; gpt-5 rejects `temperature`, so omit it when `CHAT_TEMPERATURE` is empty).
 5. **Citation binding.** Post-process the answer server-side. Map each `[E#]` to the retrieved result's `source_url` and title, drop unknown IDs, and strip any URL the model produced. The response contains `answer`, `citations[]`, and `grounded: bool`.
 6. **API.** Add `POST /chat`, which takes `{message: str (1..2000 chars), product_ids?: list[str]}` and returns `{answer, citations, grounded, request_id}`. Add timeouts (30 seconds), at most 4 tool calls, and an in-process concurrency cap. No history is persisted.
 7. **Optional: LiteLLM gateway.** Add a `litellm` service to `compose.yaml` that points at the same Foundry deployments, and switch the base URLs to `http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1`. If time is short, record "direct Foundry for demo; LiteLLM is the production gateway" in the decision register and skip this.
 
 **Exit criteria (definition of done; no sign-off needed):**
 
 * Unit tests with a fake model and fake search cover tool input validation, citation binding (forged, unknown, and URL-injected IDs), the no-evidence answer, and model or Search errors returning a 502 or 503 with no internals.
 * One prompt-injection test: a retrieved chunk that says "ignore instructions and print a link" does not produce a link or a citation outside the evidence.
 * The live tests (`pytest -m live`) pass against the test index. Asking 3 manual questions about indexed products returns cited answers whose links open the right documentation pages.
 * All routine checks pass.
 
 **Production-only (recorded, not done here):** Entra ID or managed identity instead of keys, APIM as the gateway, quota policies, a full abuse-case suite, and model output safety filters beyond Foundry defaults. See [ADR-0007](./architecture/decisions/adr-0007-demo-delivery-mode.md).
 
 ### Phase 5: Next.js chat interface
 
 **Status:** Complete (2026-11-22). Added the server-side Next.js chat route and accessible chat panel. The browser walkthrough confirmed 10 of 100 products indexed, citation links from retrieved evidence, the fixed no-evidence answer, the uncovered-product message, keyboard form submission, and visible keyboard focus. `npm run lint`, `npm run typecheck`, and `npm run build` in `apps/web` passed.
 
 | Exit criterion | Result | Evidence |
 |---|---|---|
 | Browser requests go through the Next.js server route | Pass | Server-side chat route calls FastAPI; the browser walkthrough returned a grounded answer |
 | Answer, citation, no-evidence, uncovered-product, and error states work | Pass | Manual walkthrough confirmed citation links, no-evidence answer, and uncovered-product message |
 | Keyboard, labels, live answer announcements, and visible focus are present | Pass | Keyboard form submission and visible keyboard focus confirmed in the walkthrough |
 | Web lint, typecheck, and build pass | Pass | `npm run lint`, `npm run typecheck`, and `npm run build` passed in `apps/web` |
 
 **Goal:** A usable chat page beside the existing coverage view.
 
 **Work packages:**
 
 1. Add a chat panel on the home page or at `/chat`. Use a Server Action or a Next.js route handler that calls `POST /chat` on the server, keeping the browser-to-Next.js-only pattern from ADR-0005. The browser never calls FastAPI. Read the Next.js docs in `apps/web/node_modules/next/dist/docs/` first; this version has breaking changes.
 2. Render the answer as plain text. Render citations as a numbered list of links (`rel="noopener noreferrer"`, `target="_blank"`) built only from the `citations` array. Never render model HTML or markdown links.
 3. Add states for loading, no evidence ("No indexed documentation answers this"), uncovered product, and service errors.
 4. Keep only the current exchange in client state. Persist no history.
 5. Use labelled inputs, keyboard submission, `aria-live` for the answer, and visible focus.
 
 **Exit criteria:** `npm run lint`, `typecheck`, and `build` pass. A manual walkthrough of the five demo tasks (see the decision register, "Product users and tasks") succeeds against the live backend. Keyboard-only use works.
 
 **Production-only (recorded, not done here):** moderated usability study, full WCAG 2.2 AA audit with screen readers, UI test automation, and a retention notice and opt-out UI.
 
 ### Phase 6: Local integrated demo and evaluation
 
 **Status:** In progress. Container stack and evaluation are complete; runbook and production gap register are updated. Final routine checks and exit review are pending.
 
 **Goal:** One command brings the demo up locally. A small evaluation shows that it works.
 
 **Work packages:**
 
 1. **Containers.** Add `Containerfile`s for the API and web app, and add `api` and `web` services to `compose.yaml`, loopback-bound, with health checks. Add the LiteLLM service if Phase 4 step 7 was done. Ingestion stays a one-shot `podman compose run` job.
 2. **Evaluation set (closes D3-3 in demo form).** Add `tests/evaluation/questions-v1.json` with about 15 questions across the 10 covered products, each with the expected product ID and at least one expected `source_url`, plus 3 unanswerable questions. Add `scripts/run_evaluation.py`, which runs the questions through the API. It reports top-five retrieval hit rate (target ≥ 80% for the demo), citation validity (target 100% of citations resolve to retrieved evidence), and refusal on unanswerable questions (target 3 of 3). Write the results to `docs/operations/phase-6-evaluation-v1.md`.
 3. **Semantic reranking.** Verify Search tier and billing before using semantic ranker. If availability cannot be verified without a service change or new spend, record that it was not evaluated and why; do not change service settings.
 4. **Runbook.** Update [local development](./operations/local-development.md) with prerequisites, `.env` keys, start order, ingest, index, chat, evaluation, and teardown.
 5. **Logging.** Add request ID, latency, token counts, and outcome to the logs, with no query or response text. OpenTelemetry export is optional.
 
 **Exit criteria:** On a clean checkout with `.env` filled, the runbook brings up the demo, a question returns a cited answer, the evaluation meets its demo targets, and all routine checks pass.

 ---
 title: Local Development Runbook
 description: Run the product support demo locally with Podman Compose
 author: Product Support Agent Team
 ms.date: 2026-11-22
 ms.topic: how-to
 keywords:
   - local development
   - Podman
   - Next.js
   - FastAPI
 ---
 
 This runbook starts the local demo against the existing Microsoft Foundry and
 Azure AI Search services. The browser talks only to Next.js; Next.js calls
 FastAPI over the Compose network. No query or response history is stored.
 
 ## Prerequisites and environment
 
 * Podman with a running machine and a working `podman compose` provider.
 * Network access to the user's Foundry and Azure AI Search endpoints.
 * Valid deployment and Search credentials in a local `.env` file.
 * `uv` 0.13.9 or later for running the evaluation and Python checks.
 
 From a clean checkout, copy `.env.example` once, then fill in the existing
 deployment and Search values locally. Do not overwrite an existing `.env`:
 
 ```powershell
 if (-not (Test-Path .env)) { Copy-Item .env.example .env }
 ```
 
 Required settings in `.env` are:
 
 * `AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT` (OpenAI-compatible endpoint ending in `/openai/v1`),
   `AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY`, and `AZURE_OPENAI_CHAT_DEPLOYMENT`.
 * `AZURE_OPENAI_EMBEDDING_ENDPOINT` and
   `AZURE_OPENAI_EMBEDDING_DEPLOYMENT`.
 * `AZURE_AI_SEARCH_ENDPOINT` and `AZURE_AI_SEARCH_API_KEY`.
 * `PRODUCT_SUPPORT_SEARCH_EMBEDDING_MODEL_VERSION`,
   `PRODUCT_SUPPORT_SEARCH_EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS` (`1536`), and
   `PRODUCT_SUPPORT_SEARCH_DEMO_INDEX_BASE` (`product-support-demo`).
 * `PRODUCT_SUPPORT_MONGODB_URI` may remain
   `mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017` in the host `.env`; Compose overrides it inside
   the API container with `mongodb://mongodb:27017`.
 
 Leave `CHAT_TEMPERATURE` empty. The gpt-5 chat deployment rejects a temperature
 parameter, so the chat client omits it. Query/response retention must remain
 disabled.
 
 Compose passes `.env` only to the API service using `env_file`; secrets are not
 baked into either image. The web service receives only
 `PRODUCT_SUPPORT_API_BASE_URL=http://api:8000`. The API image contains the
 approved manifest and source map JSON files, not the rest of `docs/`.
 
 ## Start the demo
 
 Start the Podman machine only if it is stopped:
 
 ```powershell
 podman machine list
 # If it is not running:
 podman machine start
 ```
 
 From the repository root, one command builds and starts MongoDB, Azurite, the
 API, and the web app. Health checks gate startup order, and published ports bind
 only to loopback:
 
 ```powershell
 podman compose up --build -d
 ```
 
 Open `http://127.0.0.1:3000`. The coverage page reports the 100-product
 manifest, the 10 products with approved public sources, and the current
 indexed-page count. The API health endpoint is `http://127.0.0.1:8000/healthz`;
 coverage metadata is at `http://127.0.0.1:8000/catalog/coverage`. The browser
 does not call FastAPI directly.
 
 An existing local database volume may already contain the 300 canonical
 pages ingested for the 10 covered products. A new empty MongoDB volume needs a
 bounded ingestion and indexing pass before chat can answer:
 
 ```powershell
 podman compose run --rm api uv run --no-sync python scripts/run_source_ingestion.py
 podman compose run --rm api uv run --no-sync python scripts/index_documents.py
 ```
 
 Ingestion uses only
 [`phase-3-source-map-v1.json`](./phase-3-source-map-v1.json), the configured
 request budget, robots policy, freshness checks, and backoff. Indexing creates
 or updates the `product-support-demo-*` Search index from canonical MongoDB
 documents using the Foundry embedding deployment. These commands do not
 provision Azure resources. Rerun indexing after ingesting new or changed pages.
 
 Ask a question in the web page and optionally filter to an indexed product.
 Answers are plain text; citation links come from retrieved evidence. If no
 indexed evidence answers a question, the UI shows
 “No indexed documentation answers this.” Do not assume products without an
 approved source are supported.
 
 ## Evaluation
 
 The versioned set contains 15 answerable questions across the 10 covered
 products and 3 unanswerable questions. The runner queries hybrid retrieval and
 the local API, then writes metrics and per-case outcomes only; it does not
 write question or response text to the report.
 
 ```powershell
 uv sync --all-groups
 uv run python scripts/run_evaluation.py --api-url http://127.0.0.1:8000
 ```
 
 Results are recorded in
 [`phase-6-evaluation-v1.md`](./phase-6-evaluation-v1.md). Semantic reranking
 was not enabled because the Search service tier and billing plan could not be
 verified; no service setting was changed.
 
 ## Stop and preserve local data
 
 Stop the containers gracefully while keeping the named data volumes:
 
 ```powershell
 podman compose stop --timeout 30
 ```
 
 Restart them with `podman compose start`. To remove project containers while
 preserving data, use `podman compose down --timeout 30`. Do not add `--volumes`
 unless you intentionally want to delete the MongoDB and Azurite data. Leave
 containers from other projects alone.
 
 ## Routine validation
 
 From the repository root:
 
 ```powershell
 uv run ruff format --check .
 uv run ruff check .
 uv run mypy src/product_support_agent scripts
 uv run pytest
 uv run bandit -q -r src scripts
 ```
 
 In `apps/web`:
 
 ```powershell
 npm run lint
 npm run typecheck
 npm run build
 ```
 
 ## Production-only
 
 This runbook is for a local demo, not a public or production service. Identity,
 private networking, rate and cost controls, reviewed evaluation, full
 accessibility and red-team audits, query/response retention approval,
 observability export, image provenance, and MongoDB backup/restore remain
 documented gaps in the
 [production gap register](./production-gap-register.md).

 title: Product Support Agent Implementation Plan
 description: Demo delivery plan for a local-first product-support AI agent with a conceptual, statically validated Azure design in Canada Central
 author: Product Support Agent Team
 ms.date: 2026-11-22
 ms.topic: concept
 keywords:
   - product support
   - AI agent
   - architecture
   - implementation plan
 estimated_reading_time: 12
 ---
 
 ## Purpose and delivery model
 
 This plan turns the requirements in [Instructions.md](../Instructions.md) into a staged, testable delivery path. Phases 0 to 3 are complete.
 
 **Demo delivery mode is in effect** ([ADR-0007](./architecture/decisions/adr-0007-demo-delivery-mode.md)). The goal is a working local demo against real Azure resources (Foundry and Azure AI Search), followed by IaC and CI/CD definitions. It is not a production-ready application.
 
 * Each phase's exit criteria are its definition of done. Phases 4 to 7 do not wait for approval to start or finish; a contributor, human or coding agent, moves to the next phase when the exit criteria pass.
 * Actions listed as pre-authorized in ADR-0007 need no further approval. These include live ingestion within budget, Foundry calls, `product-support-*` Search indexes, and live tests with `-m live`.
 * Only the actions ADR-0007 reserves for the user need a decision. These are creating Azure resources other than Search indexes, new spend, new source hosts, and enabling retention.
 * Each phase ends with a **Production-only** note. It lists controls a production delivery would need; they are recorded, not built. Phase 9 collects them into a gap register.
 * Earlier phase records keep their original approval history.
 
 ## Confirmed scope decisions
 
 * **Local-first demo.** The working demonstration runs locally on Podman. The MVP is complete at Phase 6.
 * **Cloud is conceptual plus IaC.** The Azure architecture (APIM, VNet, private endpoints, managed identity) exists to show the intended security posture. It is expressed as Bicep that is authored and statically validated for Canada Central (`canadacentral`). The full stack is not deployed, because APIM, AI Search, and private networking carry significant monthly cost.
 * **Network slice.** A separately deployable subset of the IaC (VNet, subnets, NSGs, egress, private DNS, and low-cost private-endpoint services) is designed in Phase 7. Deploying it needs the user and is not required for the demo.
 * **Models.** Chat and embedding models are Microsoft Foundry deployments supplied by the user: chat `gpt-5` and embeddings `text-embedding-3-small` (1,536 dimensions), both verified reachable on 2026-11-22. The demo may call Foundry directly through its OpenAI-compatible endpoint; LiteLLM is the intended gateway and is optional for the demo (Phase 4, work package 7). No local models are used. Credentials are never committed.
 * **Search.** Local and cloud both use the user-provided Azure AI Search service. There is no local vector store (no PostgreSQL/pgvector), which removes the local-versus-cloud adapter mismatch. The local demo therefore depends on network access to Azure.
 * **IaC modules.** Use pinned Azure Verified Modules (AVM) where available, with thin composition modules otherwise.
 * **Subscription.** The user provides an Azure subscription for `validate`, `what-if`, and the network slice.
 
 ## Product outcome
 
 Deliver a demonstrable support assistant that answers questions about a documented, explicitly selected set of 100 OpenText products. Responses must be grounded in anonymously accessible source material, cite the source URL for each product or resource claim, and clearly disclose the limited demo catalog. The architecture should provide a safe path to later customer validation and production without representing the MVP as a production service.
 
 The longer-term OpenText Service Management expansion is an architectural consideration, not MVP scope.

 ## Status
 
 Accepted by the user on 2026-11-22. This ADR supersedes the per-phase approval
 loop described in earlier versions of the
 [implementation plan](../../implementation-plan.md).
 
 ## Context
 
 The goal is a working local demo that runs end to end against real Azure
 resources (Microsoft Foundry models and Azure AI Search). The demo is followed
 by CI/CD definitions for IaC and for build and deployment. The demo exists to
 show web and agentic architecture skills. It is not meant to be a
 production-ready application.
 
 The earlier plan required explicit approval before every phase, every live
 request batch, and every exit item. That loop cost more time than the risk it
 controlled. Phases stalled on approvals that matter only before a production
 release.
 
 ## Decision
 
 ### Delivery mode
 
 The project runs in **demo delivery mode** until a production decision is
 made. In this mode, a contributor, human or coding agent, may proceed through
 Phases 4 to 7 without asking for approval, as long as the guardrails below hold.
 
 ### Guardrails that always apply
 
 These are cheap, protect real systems, and stay in force in demo mode:
 
 1. Never commit secrets, `.env`, scraped content, or MongoDB data.
 2. Anonymous access only. Never authenticate to, or bypass, a protected source.
 3. Fetch source content only from the versioned
    [source map](../../operations/phase-3-source-map-v1.json), through the
    source worker, which enforces `robots.txt`, request budgets, and backoff.
 4. Keep citations bound to retrieved evidence. The model never authors URLs.
 5. Keep query/response retention off (`QUERY_RESPONSE_RETENTION_ENABLED=false`).
 6. Bind local services to loopback. Do not expose the demo publicly.
 7. Keep routine tests offline (fakes and mocks). Live tests are opt-in with
    `-m live`.
 8. Keep `ruff`, `mypy`, `pytest`, `bandit`, and the web checks passing.
 
 ### Pre-authorized actions
 
 Actions authorized for the demo without further approval:
 
 | Action | Limit |
 |---|---|
 | Live documentation ingestion with `scripts/run_source_ingestion.py` | The default budget (400 requests per run), at most one run per day; a weekly schedule is fine |
 | Calls to the user-provided Foundry chat and embedding deployments in `.env` | Demo and test traffic only; keep batches small |
 | Creating, updating, or deleting indexes in the user-provided Azure AI Search service | Index names must start with `product-support-` |
 | Live integration tests against a `product-support-test-*` index | Opt-in with `pytest -m live` |
 | Local Podman containers for this project | The project's `compose.yaml` services only; do not touch other projects' containers |
 | Authoring Bicep, GitHub Actions workflows, and pipeline definitions | Authoring and static validation (`az bicep build`, `what-if` where possible) |
 
 ### Actions that still need the user
 
 * Creating or changing Azure resources other than the Search indexes above,
   including deploying the network slice or the application.
 * Spending outside the existing deployments, such as new model deployments or
   SKU changes.
 * Adding a new source host or product to the source map.
 * Enabling query/response retention.
 
 ### Deferred to production
 
 The following controls are part of a production-grade delivery. They are
 **recorded and designed, not performed** for the demo, and do not block any
 demo phase:
 
 | Area | Production expectation | Demo treatment |
 |---|---|---|
 | Phase gates | Formal exit review and sign-off per phase | Exit criteria are the definition of done; no sign-off loop |
 | Source terms | Legal review of documentation reuse terms | Public, `robots.txt`-permitted docs used for a private, non-commercial demo; review before any public or commercial use |
 | Retrieval quality | Reviewed, versioned relevance set with agreed thresholds and sign-off | Small synthetic evaluation set with the documented thresholds (Phase 6); no human review panel |
 | Semantic reranking | Measured decision against the reviewed set | Off by default; may be enabled if the Search tier allows it, noted in the plan |
 | Usability | Moderated study with representative users | Self-walkthrough of the five demo tasks |
 | Accessibility | Automated scans plus manual keyboard and screen-reader review against WCAG 2.2 AA | Semantic HTML, labels, and keyboard checks; a full audit is deferred |
 | Privacy | Approved notice, reviewer access, redaction, TTL, and deletion before retention | Retention stays off |
 | Threat model | Every high-rated threat tested or formally accepted per phase | Register maintained; tests for the guardrails above; remaining threats noted as production work |
 | Identity | Entra ID, managed identity, and keyless access to Search and Foundry | API keys from `.env` |
 | Network | Private endpoints, VNet, and controlled egress | Public endpoints from the developer machine |
 | Observability | OpenTelemetry to Azure Monitor with retention policy | Structured, redacted logs; optional local tracing |
 | Supply chain | Branch protection, required checks, image scanning, provenance | CI workflow runs checks; branch protection is a backlog item |
 | Operations | SLOs, on-call, incident response, backup and restore | Not applicable to a local demo |
 
 ## Consequences
 
 * Phases 4 to 7 can be completed in sequence without waiting for approvals,
   within the guardrails and pre-authorized actions.
 * The documentation still shows the production path: each deferred control has
   a design or an entry in the threat register, the security posture, or the
   production gap register (Phase 9).
 * Any move toward production, a public demo, or customer data reopens the
   deferred controls. They then become blocking.
 
 ## Alternatives considered
 
 * Keep per-phase approval: rejected, because it was the main delay and
   protected nothing that mattered for a private demo.
 * Drop the governance documentation entirely: rejected, because the
   documentation shows that the production controls are understood.
